name: Al Qusais Archaeological Site

location.proximity: Near Dubai International Airport; close to the Dubai–Sharjah border

type: Archaeological Site — Prehistoric Necropolis and Settlement

periods.name: Late Bronze Age — Wadi Suq Period

key_findings: First systematic exposure of the Bronze and Iron Age necropolis
Identification of 267 simple pit graves and 3 communal tombs
Discovery of the 'Mound of Serpents' occupation area
Copper alloy snake figurines and snake-decorated ceramics recovered
Evidence of a columned hall structure interpreted as a possible Iron Age II temple

excavation_history.organisation: Dubai Department of Antiquities and Heritage
key_findings: 101 additional burial pits excavated in the necropolis area
Rich assemblages of grave goods recovered but not fully published at the time
Human skeletal remains identified, though publication was delayed ~30 years
excavation_history.reference: Qandil, H. (1993). Archaeological Report of al-Qusais 1991–1993. Dubai Municipality: Unpublished Report.

excavation_history.organisation: Dubai Culture Authority & Arts / Sanisera International Archaeology Institute
key_findings: Nine new burial pits excavated; 19 new pits identified in total
Reassessment and first systematic study of 1990s unanalysed material
Grave goods confirmed: copper daggers, soft-stone vessels (chlorite/steatite), pottery, jewellery, beads, shells
Human remains formally identified and analysed
Geomorphological and palaeoenvironmental study of the prehistoric landscape conducted
Chronological framework refined for Bronze-to-Iron Age cultural transition
Infant and child burials studied — 7 child remains (aged ~2–6) found in 126 excavated graves
excavation_history.publication: Valente, T., Contreras, F., Vila, B., Fernández, A., Al Ali, B., Radwan Karim, M. B., & Zein, H. M. (2023). The necropolis of Al Qusais (Dubai, UAE): preliminary results on the 2020 excavation and data reassessment from the 70s and 90s excavations. Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies, 52, 355–372.

excavation_history.organisation: Dubai Culture Authority & Arts / Sanisera International Archaeology Institute
key_findings: Updated chronology of burial activity published
Total confirmed burials: 267 simple graves + 3 communal graves (290+ total)
Site recognised as one of the most important prehistoric sites in the Arabian Peninsula

site_areas.name: Bronze and Iron Age Necropolis
site_areas.description: The primary burial ground comprising hundreds of pit graves and communal tombs spanning the Late Bronze Age through to the Iron Age. Graves contain flexed skeletons in lateral positions alongside rich grave goods.

site_areas.name: Mound of Serpents (Tell al-Hayat)
site_areas.description: An Iron Age II occupation area (c. 1000–800 BCE) distinguished by the discovery of numerous copper alloy snake figurines and ceramics with snake motifs. Associated with a columned hall structure interpreted as a possible early temple or ritual space. Parallels exist at Bithnah (Fujairah), Masafi, and sites in Oman.
site_areas.cultural_significance: Potential evidence of serpent veneration or ritual cult in south-eastern Arabia

metal: Copper alloy snake figurines (diagnostic of the Mound of Serpents area)

cultural_significance.regional_importance: One of the most important prehistoric archaeological sites in the Arabian Peninsula, providing crucial evidence for the Late Bronze Age and Iron Age in south-eastern Arabia.
cultural_significance.burial_practices: The site offers detailed insights into funerary customs, community structure, and demographic patterns (including infant mortality) of Bronze-to-Iron Age populations in the Gulf region.
cultural_significance.trade_connections: Grave goods indicate active trade connections across the Arabian Peninsula and beyond, consistent with the broader Wadi Suq cultural horizon.
cultural_significance.cultural_transition: The site is a key reference for understanding the poorly-differentiated cultural shift from the Bronze Age to the Iron Age in the UAE.
cultural_significance.serpent_cult: The Mound of Serpents provides rare evidence for possible serpent-related ritual practices in Iron Age II south-eastern Arabia, with parallels at Bithnah (Fujairah) and sites in Oman and Bahrain.
cultural_significance.demography: Analysis of 126 excavated graves reveals evidence of familial burial customs, with children interred alongside adults, providing data on Bronze Age community demographics and early childhood survival.

conservation_status.threats: Significant portions of the site were destroyed by urbanisation following Dubai's oil-driven expansion in the 1970s–1980s. The site is now surrounded by modern urban development.
conservation_status.protection: Managed by Dubai Culture Authority & Arts.
conservation_status.current_status: Partially preserved; active research and excavation programme ongoing as of 2024.
